Q2: Allocate to Patient A (Floor 4, post-surgical, 7.9). Patient A's score is markedly higher (7.9 vs 6.8) and post-surgical deterioration can escalate rapidly into hemorrhage, dehiscence, or sepsis, which demands ICU-level monitoring. Q3: Allocate to Patient A (ER Bay 1, stroke, 8.8). Stroke at 8.8 is the highest urgency in this scenario, and stroke outcomes are brutally time-dependent, with every minute of brain ischemia costing viable tissue. Patient B (MI, 8.6) is also very serious, but MI has established ER-based reperfusion pathways, whereas stroke needs the ICU's neuro-monitoring now.
Q4: Allocate to Patient A (Floor 2, pneumonia, 7.1). Patient A clearly needs it more (7.1 vs 5.5) and pneumonia can tip into respiratory failure, which is exactly what ICU-level support exists to prevent. Patient B (observation, 5.5) sits at the bottom of the serious band and can wait on a monitored floor bed without meaningful risk.
Q5: Allocate to Patient B (ER Bay 9, overdose, 8.4). Overdose at 8.4 is the more urgent presentation, since airway protection and ventilation needs can crash suddenly and unpredictably. Q6: Allocate to Patient A (Stepdown, CHF exacerbation, 6.8). Patient A has the higher score (6.8 vs 6.5) and is already on Stepdown, signaling clinical deterioration that is trending the wrong way toward pulmonary edema or cardiogenic shock. Patient B (asthma, 6.5) can continue on ER nebulizer therapy and observation a while longer.
Q7: Allocate to Patient A (ER Bay 8, trauma, 7.5). Patient A is the only waiting patient, and at 7.5 sits in the serious band where trauma can decompensate without warning from occult bleeding. An empty ICU bed with a waiting trauma patient is a system failure, so the bed goes to Patient A.
Q8: Allocate to Patient A (Cath Lab, post-PCI, 8.7). Patient A is by far the more urgent case (8.7 vs 7.2) and the immediate post-PCI window carries real risk of acute stent thrombosis, arrhythmia, or access-site bleeding, all of which need ICU-level surveillance. Patient B (COPD, 7.2) is serious but manageable on the floor with bronchodilators and monitoring while waiting.
Q9: Allocate to Patient A (ER Bay 10, cellulitis, 5.9). Both patients sit in the serious-but-low band, but Patient A has the higher score (5.9 vs 5.6) and cellulitis can progress to sepsis if antibiotics fail, so ICU-capable observation is the safer placement. Patient B (dehydration, 5.6) can be managed with IV fluids in the ER or on a floor bed while waiting.
